strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: bridging perturbation-based (causally grounded) and learning-based (amortized) explainability by directly optimizing differentiable surrogates of the Deletion/Insertion metrics, rather than distilling heuristic teachers or optimizing restrictive surrogate objectives.

Technically sound core idea: reformulating metric optimization as permutation learning with a Gumbel-Sinkhorn relaxation of sorting and cumulative-sum soft top-k masks is elegant, and the observation that the metrics depend only on rank ordering justifies the relaxation.

Practical training recipe is well designed: region-level permutation, sampled perturbation steps, grid augmentation, and a smoothness regularizer address both the computational burden and shortcut/artifact risks of per-pixel optimization.

Strong and unusually thorough empirical evaluation: full 50K ImageNet validation split, three classifiers (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt Small), eight faithfulness metrics, averaging over three reference-image modes, separate reporting for predicted vs. ground-truth classes, ablations of refinement steps T and perturbation steps S, and a comparison under the MDA evaluation protocol (Table 4).

Favorable efficiency/quality trade-off: T=0 inference is comparable to propagation methods (~0.016s) while outperforming much slower per-sample metric optimization (MDA at ~13.6s), and T=3 refinement further improves all metrics at modest cost.

Interesting OOD application (Appendix A.3): test-time refinement revealing an injected shortcut in a fine-tuned model demonstrates the method can adapt to unseen model behaviors, supporting the claim of causal grounding.
Honest limitations section discussing per-model retraining cost, proxy-metric shortcomings, and the need for training data access; code availability is promised, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity risk (Goodhart's law): the training objective and a large portion of the evaluation are the same Deletion/Insertion metrics. The additional metrics (Positive/Negative perturbation, ADP, PIC) are themselves perturbation-based and conceptually similar, so the evaluation is still dominated by the very objective being optimized. No metric-independent validation (e.g., point/game-theoretic faithfulness checks, human studies, or localization against ground-truth segmentations) is provided.

Heavy dependence on a very strong frozen explainer backbone (DINOv3 ViT-L/16, larger than the ViT-B targets being explained). The paper does not isolate how much of the performance comes from the target model versus prior knowledge encoded in the explainer backbone; e.g., a weaker or randomly initialized decoder/backbone ablation, or explaining models with architectures very different from the backbone, would strengthen the claim that the attributions are truly target-model-faithful.

Per-target-model retraining limits scalability and applicability; the claim that refinement (T>0) 'can be employed to resolve such data issues' is not substantiated by a controlled experiment on refinement without any training data (the OOD experiment still uses an explainer trained on related data).

Training/inference resolution mismatch is under-analyzed: training optimizes region-level (G×G grid) permutations while inference produces pixel-level maps; the paper does not quantify how the learned pixel-level ranking relates to the region-level objective beyond qualitative observations.

Several methodological details that affect reproducibility and interpretation are underspecified in the main text: attribution normalization for the similarity matrix in Eq. (6) (scores a are matched against target positions in [0,1]), temperature schedule details, Sinkhorn iteration sensitivity, and variance/confidence intervals for reported AUCs across the 50K-image evaluation.

Experiments are confined to ImageNet classification at 224×224; generalization to other datasets, tasks (segmentation, detection), or model families (Swin, CNNs in the main text) is not demonstrated, so claims of broad applicability rest on limited evidence.

Novelty is moderate in isolation: Gumbel-Sinkhorn permutation learning, DPT decoders, and metric-driven attribution (MDA) all exist; the contribution is primarily their combination and engineering of an efficient amortized scheme rather than a new fundamental mechanism.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and technically clean: recasting the non-differentiable Deletion/Insertion metrics as a permutation learning problem and relaxing sorting/top-k via Gumbel-Sinkhorn is a novel and sensible bridge between perturbation-based and learning-based attribution, going beyond surrogate objectives or distillation used in prior amortized explainers.

The method delivers a genuinely useful operating point: single-forward-pass attribution (0.016s) with faithfulness competitive or superior to per-sample optimization methods like MDA (13.6s), plus an optional, well-characterized test-time refinement (T=3) that further improves all metrics — the compute-quality tradeoff is clearly quantified (Fig. 3a, runtime tables).

Evaluation is substantially more thorough than typical: two ViT variants and a ConvNeXt classifier (demonstrating architecture-agnostic applicability in the appendix), full 50K ImageNet validation split, both predicted- and ground-truth class targets, averaging over three reference images, complementary metrics beyond the training objective (Positive/Negative perturbation, ADP, PIC, composite faithfulness), a fair re-evaluation on MDA's official protocol/subset, ablations on S and T, and a controlled shortcut-detection experiment (Fig. 5) that is a nice, convincing demonstration of OOD adaptability via refinement.

Practical design choices (region-level permutation, perturbation-step sampling, grid augmentation, smoothing regularization) are well justified and directly address the pixel-artifact/shortcut overfitting concern that plagues metric optimization.
Limitations are honestly discussed: per-model retraining cost, proxy-metric sensitivity, and the requirement for representative training data.
weaknesses: The explainer relies on a very strong, heavily pretrained frozen DINOv3 ViT-L backbone. The paper does not ablate the backbone, so it is unclear how much of the reported fidelity comes from the metric-driven objective versus simply reusing DINOv3's excellent dense features. A weaker backbone ablation (or comparing explainers built on the target model's own features) would substantially strengthen the causal claim.

There is a circularity risk: the training objective is a differentiable surrogate of Deletion/Insertion, and the headline metrics in Tables 1-2 are exactly Deletion/Insertion AUCs. While Positive/Negative, ADP, and PIC provide some independent evidence, and the maps look plausible, the paper would benefit from at least one evaluation axis structurally decoupled from perturbation AUCs (e.g., point game/weakly supervised localization against annotations, or downstream model debugging utility).

Train/evaluation granularity mismatch: training operates on G×G region grids (7–28 regions) with soft masks, while evaluation is pixel-level with hard masks. The paper argues grid augmentation mitigates this, but the potential gap between the optimized surrogate and the reported metric is not directly analyzed (e.g., a train-objective vs. true-metric gap measurement).

Per-explainer training cost (one epoch over ImageNet-1K) is not reported, making it hard to judge the true amortization break-even point versus per-sample methods like MDA for practitioners with smaller data or many models.

A few results are mixed and under-discussed: e.g., TIS retains better Insertion/ADP/PIC at T=0 in Table 1, and the explanation of why the zero-shot method beats per-sample optimization ('more precise alignment with the input') is asserted rather than evidenced experimentally.
Scope of validation is effectively ImageNet classification only; generalization to other domains or tasks is untested, which tempers claims of a general framework, though this is common for the area.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the observation that Deletion/Insertion metrics depend only on the ranking of attribution values (not their magnitudes) enables a principled reformulation of metric optimization as permutation learning, which is a genuinely novel angle for amortized explainability.

Technically sound core method: the Gumbel-Sinkhorn relaxation of sorting, soft top-k mask construction via cumulative sums of the soft permutation matrix, and the practical training strategies (region-based permutation, perturbation-step sampling, grid augmentation, smoothness regularization) are well designed and clearly described.

Strong empirical evidence: evaluation on the full ImageNet validation set (50K images) across three classifiers (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt Small), multiple faithfulness metrics beyond the training objective (Positive/Negative perturbation, ADP, PIC), both predicted- and ground-truth-class targets, averaging over three reference images, per-reference-image breakdowns, and evaluation under the MDA protocol. AHA dominates on Deletion and composite faithfulness while being orders of magnitude faster than per-sample optimization (MDA).

Attractive practical trade-off: single forward pass at T=0 comparable to Grad-CAM runtime, with an optional few-step test-time refinement that monotonically improves quality; the OOD shortcut-detection experiment (Fig. 5) is a compelling demonstration of refinement transferring to unseen models/data.

Good reproducibility posture: implementation details, architecture description (appendix A.1), hyperparameters, ablations on refinement steps T and perturbation steps S, stated code availability, and honest limitations section.
Well-written with a thorough related-work section that correctly positions the method against propagation-, perturbation-, and learning-based approaches.
weaknesses: Circularity concern: the method is trained to directly maximize differentiable surrogates of Deletion/Insertion and is then evaluated primarily on those same metrics (and their variants). The authors partly mitigate this with Positive/Negative perturbation tests, ADP/PIC, and qualitative results, and the OOD experiment is reassuring, but a human-grounded evaluation (e.g., pointing game, segmentation masks) or an independent faithfulness measure not related to the training objective would substantially strengthen the claim that the maps are genuinely more faithful rather than better optimized for the metric.

The explainer uses a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone that is considerably larger than the target classifiers being explained (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt-Small). While inference is cheap, the amortization cost and memory footprint of training are not quantified, so the practical cost story is incomplete.

Scope of evidence is limited to ImageNet-scale classification. No results on other tasks (detection, segmentation), other data domains, or larger/other transformer families (Swin, etc.), which limits generality claims of the 'architecture-agnostic' framing (ConvNeXt in the appendix helps but is a single point).

Each new target model requires full explainer retraining; although acknowledged, there is no measurement of this training cost or of how much the learned prior transfers across target models (only the small shortcut case suggests some transferability via refinement).

On Insertion specifically, TIS remains competitive with or better than AHA at T=0 in several settings (Tables 1-2), so the improvement claim is strongest for Deletion and composite faithfulness rather than uniform dominance; this nuance could be stated more explicitly.

Some details affecting reproducibility are deferred or underspecified in the main text (e.g., temperature schedule τ_final, target-position scaling p = (1/N)[N,...,1] sensitivity, how ground-truth-class maps are obtained when the class differs from training targets).
